name: AI-enabled borescope training at AEMTC
summary: China's Aero Engine Maintenance Training Center, set up in 1996 through a partnership involving GE Aerospace, Safran Aircraft Engines, CFM International, China Aviation Supplies and Chinese aviation authorities, is introducing AI-enabled borescope training and mixed-reality teaching methods, MRO Business Today reported on October 14. The center says the aim is to make training more efficient and accurate while keeping human judgment at the center of inspection and maintenance decisions. Based at the Civil Aviation Flight University of China in Guanghan, Sichuan, the 7,500 square meter center has 10 training engines covering nine models, including the CFM56 family, LEAP-1A, LEAP-1B, LEAP-1C and CF34-10A, and had trained about 17,500 people from more than 120 airlines, MROs and manufacturers by the end of 2025. The report cites IATA figures projecting annual LEAP shop visits to rise from about 600 to 800 in 2025 to 1,800 to 2,000 by 2030. No details were given on how the AI training works.

whyItMatters: Borescope inspection is one of the slowest skills to build, and a technician who misreads a blade can cost an engine removal or miss a real defect. If AI can show a trainee what good and bad findings look like on hundreds of examples, new hires reach a useful level sooner, which is billable time for an MRO short of engine people. When you hire, ask candidates what borescope training they have had, and ask training providers how much hands-on time sits behind any AI module.
